summary:
Forest Watch is a web map that shows what a wildfire does to a forest. We took open NISAR L-band radar data from NASA and ISRO and turned it into simple, coloured layers for three fire regions: Hürtgenwald in Germany, and Monthermé and Gironde in France. Users pick a region, pick a layer such as vegetation or forest, and move through time on a timeline. A Compare button shows two dates side by side, so the change before and after the fire is visible at a glance. A Learn mode explains how radar works in short steps.

The challenge asks us to use SAR data to reveal changes on Earth. Radar sees through smoke and clouds and returns to the same place about every 12 days, which makes it ideal for tracking fire damage and regrowth. But the raw files are huge and need expert software. Forest Watch removes that barrier: it runs in any browser, with no login and no install.

This matters because wildfire risk is growing in Europe, and the people affected, such as pupils, local communities and foresters, should be able to see the damage in their own region for themselves.
details:
What it does

Forest Watch is a web map that shows what a wildfire does to a forest. It turns NISAR L-band radar data into simple, coloured layers that anyone can read. You pick a fire region (Hürtgenwald in Germany, Monthermé or Gironde in France), pick a layer such as vegetation or forest, and move through time on a timeline. A Compare button puts two dates side by side with a swipe line, so the change is visible at a glance.

How it works

NISAR sends radar pulses to the ground and measures the echo. Radar works at night and passes through smoke and clouds, and the satellite returns to the same spot about every 12 days. Dense forest sends back a strong echo from trunks and branches; burned or cleared forest sends back a weak one. We download the open NISAR data from the Alaska Satellite Facility, cut out each region, and convert the measurements into small map layers. The app compares the echo before and after the fire and marks where the forest signal dropped and stayed low. A Learn mode explains radar in six short steps, without jargon.

Benefits

Radar data is free, but the raw files are huge and need expert software. Forest Watch needs no login, no install and no server: it runs as a plain web page in any browser. Layers are named by what they show, not by technical terms.

Intended impact

We want pupils, teachers, local communities and foresters to see fire damage in their own region and to follow the regrowth after reforestation. The same method can be applied to any fire that NISAR has observed.

Tools

Python (asf-search, h5py, NumPy, pyproj, FastAPI) for downloading and processing the data. HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet for the map, on an OpenStreetMap base map. Data: NISAR (NASA and ISRO) via the Alaska Satellite Facility; Sentinel-2 (ESA Copernicus) for optical images. GitHub for the code.

Creativity

Instead of a dashboard for experts, we built a map a school class can use in a few minutes, with a guided Learn mode and a before/after swipe.

What we considered

We only claim what the data supports. The radar signal is a proxy for forest structure, not a direct biomass measurement. Rain and soil moisture also change the signal, radar cannot tell fire from felling, and the data are provisional. The app states these limits openly.
